headline: Iran says six tankers have struck mines near Hormuz since Sunday
standfirst: The Revolutionary Guards say six tankers have caught fire after striking mines near Hormuz since Sunday, as a third American aircraft carrier reaches the region. Ukraine launches its biggest drone attack on Russia, ASEAN and China fail to conclude their maritime code of conduct, COP31 stalls over finance, and Sudan's army advances in Kordofan.

essentials.title: Iran says six tankers have hit mines near Hormuz as a third American carrier arrives
essentials.standfirst: The Revolutionary Guards say six tankers have caught fire after striking mines near Hormuz since Sunday, a day after a claimed drone attack on Bahrain. A third American aircraft carrier has reached the region, and Tehran rules out any nuclear inspections until the war is over.
body: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Monday 16 November that two more tankers had struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz, bringing to six the number of ships set ablaze since Sunday according to Iranian state media, a day after they claimed a six-drone attack on the Riffa base in Bahrain.

The American carrier Theodore Roosevelt has arrived in the region, joining the George H. W. Bush and the George Washington, while a Panama-flagged tanker, the ON Phoenix, was hit by an unknown projectile off Oman without casualties, The Times of Israel reports.

Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran's deputy foreign minister, rules out any IAEA access to nuclear sites until the war has permanently ended, while Abbas Araghchi, the foreign minister, said in Islamabad that the Economic Cooperation Organisation backs an Iranian plan to reopen Hormuz within two days, on conditions.

figure.compare: against $71.66 on 26 February, before the war

positions.wants: An end to the American naval blockade and to sanctions, the release of its frozen assets, a halt to hostilities on every front and a formal declaration that the war is over, according to Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.
To keep Iranian ports under blockade and tighten sanctions, the Trump administration having not yet formally answered the conditions passed on by the Qatari mediator.
Full implementation of Security Council Resolution 2817, which condemned Iran's attacks on Bahrain and other countries in the region.

analysis.title: A low-intensity war that could spiral
analysis.text: The fighting has subsided, but no agreement has ended the war that began with American and Israeli strikes on 28 February: Iran still sporadically targets American bases in the Gulf, while Washington throttles its economy with the blockade. Friday's claim against Bahrain, home to the headquarters of America's Fifth Fleet, was the first aimed at American military installations in a Gulf state since early September, according to Reuters. Tehran insists that it alone, with Oman, controls the Strait of Hormuz, which America disputes. The danger now lies in miscalculation, argues Saeid Golkar, a political scientist quoted by Al Jazeera: limited exchanges can escalate at any moment.

keys.title: The Saudi front
keys.text: The Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted two ballistic missiles fired by Yemen's Houthis towards Riyadh on Sunday, as well as three drones over the Eastern Province. Riyadh expressed its “full solidarity” with Bahrain.

keys.title: The Gulf's bill
keys.text: The Arab Gulf monarchies demanded on Friday that Iran pay “full compensation” for the thousands of missiles and drones fired since February. They want the UN Security Council to hold Tehran to account.

keys.title: Unverifiable claims
keys.text: The Guards have given neither the names nor the flags of the tankers, and no maritime authority has confirmed the explosions. Only the ON Phoenix incident, off Oman, has been reported by Britain's UKMTO and the security firm Vanguard.

context.t: War breaks out between America, Israel and Iran.
The Guards claim to have destroyed an American radar in Bahrain, which Washington denies.
Two tankers strike mines south of Hormuz, according to the Guards' navy.
Nationwide alerts in Bahrain; Tehran claims a six-drone attack on the Riffa base.

essentials.title: Ukraine launches its biggest drone attack on Russia, reaching as far as the Crimean bridge
essentials.standfirst: Moscow says it intercepted 1,336 Ukrainian drones in one night, a record since the invasion began, nearly 600 of them heading for the Moscow region. The Kremlin reports “insignificant” damage to the Kerch bridge, while Kyiv presses for Starshield restrictions to be lifted.
body: Russia's defence ministry said on Monday 16 November that it had intercepted 1,336 Ukrainian drones in a single night, the highest number it has claimed since the invasion, about 600 of them aimed at the Moscow region according to the city's mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, the Associated Press reports.

The Kerch bridge linking Crimea to Russia was targeted, with the Kremlin's spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, describing the damage as “insignificant”, while Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukraine has knocked out more than 55% of Russia's refining capacity and condemns the speed limits on SpaceX's Starshield terminals.

Russia fired more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 glide bombs and 15 missiles at Ukraine in a single week, according to Ukraine's president, and its strikes on the Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions left hundreds of thousands of homes without power as winter approaches.

analysis.title: A dependency turned into leverage
analysis.text: Ukraine's army relies on both commercial Starlink and Starshield, which the Kyiv Independent credits for the success of its strikes on Russian logistics at medium range. That the terminals are throttled precisely over occupied territory gives the matter a political edge: Mr Zelensky sees it as a partial acknowledgment that those areas are not Ukrainian, and doubts that the limit is purely technical, even though America's secretary of state, Marco Rubio, had assured him that Starshield was more a matter for the American government. The restriction comes as Moscow concentrates its Shaheds on electrical substations, as in previous winters, and as Washington discusses a territorial compromise in the Donbas with Kyiv.

keys.title: The response in Congress
keys.text: The bipartisan Ukraine caucus in the American Congress has demanded a full explanation from the Trump administration and SpaceX. It wants full Starshield access restored to Ukraine's armed forces immediately.

keys.title: Ukraine's strikes in Russia
keys.text: In Azov, in Rostov region, three people were wounded by drones, and Ukraine's army says it hit two oil depots there. Six people were wounded in Krasnodar region, according to local authorities.

keys.title: The American proposal
keys.text: Mr Zelensky revealed that Washington had floated NATO membership for Ukraine in exchange for a withdrawal from the Donbas. He demands guarantees at least equivalent to Article 5 and refuses to recognise any occupied territory as Russian.

essentials.title: ASEAN and China fail to conclude their code of conduct for the South China Sea
essentials.standfirst: Meeting in Manila, South-East Asian countries could not finish the text promised for 2026 with Beijing, though some 80% of it has been provisionally agreed. The Philippine chair hands the file to Singapore, before Donald Trump arrives on Tuesday.
body: The Philippines' foreign secretary, Ma. Theresa Lazaro, acknowledged on Sunday 15 November, on the sidelines of the 49th ASEAN summit in Manila, that the bloc and China had not concluded a code of conduct for the South China Sea, despite provisional agreement on about 80% of the draft's paragraphs, Reuters reports.

Still unresolved are whether the text will be legally binding and what area it will cover, with Beijing claiming almost all of a sea through which half the world's merchant ships pass, despite a 2016 arbitral ruling it rejects, against rival claims from the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia.

Singapore, which takes over the ASEAN chair next year, inherits a text that has been under negotiation for more than two decades, while Donald Trump is due in Manila on Tuesday for a special ASEAN-US summit before heading to Shenzhen for APEC.

figure.label: of the draft code's paragraphs provisionally agreed, according to Manila
figure.compare: after more than two decades of talks

positions.wants: A code that respects the rights of countries outside the region, according to the foreign ministry's spokesman, Dominic Xavier Imperial, with Ms Lazaro calling the document 80% complete.
A “rational and unified” voice from the Philippines, China's foreign minister, Wang Yi, having asked Manila to rein in its politicians.

next.t: Special ASEAN-US summit in Manila, attended by Donald Trump.

analysis.title: A text hostage to Sino-Philippine relations
analysis.text: In 2023 ASEAN and Chinese foreign ministers gave themselves three years to reach a deal, a deadline that fell during the Philippine chairmanship. But Manila, locked in an open dispute with Beijing over the reefs it claims, was awkwardly placed: a strong text would have looked imposed on China, a weak one would have damaged Ferdinand Marcos Jr's government, says Aries Arugay, a political scientist quoted by Al Jazeera. Relations have soured in recent months, amid insults traded between the defence secretary, Gilberto Teodoro, who is barred from entering China, and China's ambassador in Manila. Divisions within ASEAN, notably over the scope of the code, also weigh, according to Collin Koh, a Singaporean researcher quoted by Reuters.

keys.title: The one settled point
keys.text: Of the four main areas of disagreement, negotiators settled only how the code relates to the 2002 declaration, whose principles it is to incorporate. Ms Lazaro says she is leaving Singapore a document “almost 80% complete”.

keys.title: The summit's other results
keys.text: Leaders signed ASEAN's digital economy framework agreement and a memorandum of understanding on a regional power grid. They also adopted a declaration on the fair recruitment of migrant workers.

context.t: ASEAN and China sign a declaration on the conduct of parties in the South China Sea.

essentials.title: Halfway through COP31, climate finance still divides rich and developing countries
essentials.standfirst: The developing countries' bloc rejected a text on climate finance as too weak in Antalya on Saturday, just as ministers take over from negotiators. The coalition to move away from fossil fuels presses on without Colombia, one of its founders.
body: The Group of 77 and China on Saturday 14 November rejected in Antalya the latest text on the work programme for climate finance, calling it too weak, as COP31 enters its second week with the arrival of ministers, according to Climate Action Network.

African countries have made tripling adaptation finance to at least $120bn a year by 2035 their priority, but the European Union, Japan and Norway object to that benchmark, while the mechanism for a just transition amounts, for now, to a knowledge centre and an annual meeting.

Simon Stiell, the UN's climate chief, calls progress “constructive” and urges delegations to avoid stalling tactics before the scheduled close on Friday, while the coalition launched in Santa Marta to move away from fossil fuels carries on without Colombia, which left it after Abelardo de la Espriella's election.

figure.label: requested by 119 countries from the loss and damage fund
figure.compare: against roughly $600m received, according to Climate Action Network

positions.wants: A more ambitious text on climate finance, the one tabled on Saturday having been rejected as too weak, while obligations under Article 9.1 of the Paris agreement are once again in dispute.
To drop references to tripling adaptation finance, and to avoid detailed guidance for the loss and damage fund, citing the independence of its board.
Resources that match the needs of the loss and damage fund, which has received requests for $2.8bn against roughly $600m in contributions.

items.name: Antalya
items.note: Host city of COP31, where ministers and negotiators are starting the second week.

analysis.title: Belém's promise put to the test
analysis.text: COP30 in Belém launched a just-transition mechanism and promised to triple adaptation finance; Antalya is meant to give both substance. Yet the first text on the just transition offers mainly a portal, reports and an annual meeting, with no explicit commitment of money, which civil-society groups denounce. The presidency is shared: Australia, through its climate minister, Chris Bowen, steers the negotiations, while Turkey runs the action agenda. Some large emerging economies also reject the idea of an overarching cover decision setting sectoral goals, such as electrification, which the EU may no longer describe as “clean”, according to Climate Home News.

keys.title: The Santa Marta coalition
keys.text: Launched in Colombia in April by some 60 governments frustrated by the slow pace of COPs, it is due to present a progress report this week. Ireland and Tuvalu are set to take the lead after Bogotá's departure.

keys.title: Electrification
keys.text: Turkey is championing a voluntary pledge to raise electricity's share of final energy consumption from 23% to 35% by 2035. At least 14 countries have backed it, according to Climate Home News.

essentials.title: In Sudan, the army regains ground in Kordofan, where drone strikes are killing civilians
essentials.standfirst: Sudan's army and its Darfuri allies have retaken several towns in West Kordofan and loosened the grip on El Obeid. Civilians are paying the price of the offensive, caught between drones and paramilitary attacks.
body: Sudan's army and allied Darfuri forces have in recent days retaken several strategic towns in West Kordofan, including Al-Khuwei, breaking the siege that the Rapid Support Forces had imposed on El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, according to Al Jazeera.

General Hemedti's paramilitaries still hold En Nahud, a gold-mining town where they have killed ten civilians since Thursday, according to a local relief group quoted by Anadolu, while drone strikes have killed at least 15 civilians in the region in recent days, according to the Sudanese outlet Darfur24.

Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera expect the paramilitaries to fall back towards Darfur, their tribal heartland, as the UN describes Kordofan as the epicentre of the conflict and most humanitarian operations there have been suspended.

analysis.title: Kordofan, the lock between Khartoum and Darfur
analysis.text: After El Fasher fell in October 2025, the Rapid Support Forces controlled most of Darfur and threatened El Obeid, the gateway to central Sudan. Retaking towns in West Kordofan opens routes for the army towards Babanusa and Darfur, and brings it closer to the country's oil heartland: according to the economist Mohamed al-Nayer, quoted by Al Jazeera, the Heglig and Balila fields provide 90% of Sudan's output, and the region's stability also determines South Sudan's exports. Both sides take turns claiming unverifiable victories, and several towns have changed hands more than once since the start of the month, according to Asharq Al-Awsat.

keys.title: Conflicting claims
keys.text: The spokesman for the Joint Force allied with the army says it retook four towns in early November and destroyed 40 combat vehicles. Media close to the paramilitaries insist, on the contrary, that they pushed the army back towards El Obeid.

keys.title: Civilians in the line of fire
keys.text: According to Darfur24, drones have in recent days struck a passenger car, a fuel market in Foga, a convoy carrying farm produce and a motorised tricycle. Children are among the victims.

brief.text: Allies of Benjamin Netanyahu have told Gadi Eisenkot's team that Likud would accept a unity government without Itamar Ben-Gvir's party, according to the daily Israel Hayom, a report Likud denies.
Nearly $20m in cash, hidden on farms and buried in forests, has been found in the investigation into Miklos Sesztak, a former minister under Viktor Orban accused of corruption, who denies wrongdoing.
Italy's data-protection authority has fined Meta €805m for accessing Android users' photos and videos without their consent; the company says it will appeal.

American air-traffic control has stabilised after a nationwide outage, according to the Federal Aviation Administration, but airlines expected to cancel 4,000 to 5,000 of some 41,000 scheduled flights.
